headline: Zoning kept out factories. Then apartments.
dek: In 1916 New York wrote the first US zoning code to bring light back to its streets.

slides.label: The bright idea
slides.title: A shadow over Broadway
slides.text: Manhattan in the 1910s had crowded tenements with little light or air, and factories creeping toward Fifth Avenue. In 1915 the 538-foot Equitable Building went up and cast a seven-acre shadow on its neighbors.
slides.alt: The Equitable Building, a huge flat-topped office block, towering over Trinity Church and its neighbors in lower Manhattan
slides.credit: Equitable Building, New York City, 1915. Library of Congress. Public domain.

slides.label: It worked
slides.title: America's first zoning code
slides.text: Edward M. Bassett, a lawyer and former congressman, chaired the commission behind New York's 1916 code, the first comprehensive zoning in the US. It capped heights and kept factories out of residential districts.
slides.alt: Charcoal drawing of a stepped skyscraper mass, its towers narrowing in setbacks as they rise
slides.credit: Study of the largest building the 1916 zoning law allowed, 1922. Hugh Ferriss. Cooper Hewitt. Public domain.

slides.label: Wait, what?
slides.title: Further than he went
slides.text: Bassett warned that banning apartments from home districts might not survive in court. In 1926 the Supreme Court upheld a code that did, in Euclid, Ohio, calling an apartment house near homes very often "a mere parasite."

slides.label: The backfire
slides.title: Homes far from everything
slides.statLabel: homes the US was short in 2022, a Moody's estimate the White House cited
slides.text: As zoning spread, codes kept homes, shops and jobs in separate districts. The EPA noted in 2001 that this leaves people relying on cars. In 2022 the White House said exclusionary zoning inflates home prices.
also: Source: White House Housing Supply Action Plan fact sheet, May 2022

slides.label: Could anyone have seen it coming?
slides.title: A judge warned. The cars came later.
slides.text: In 1924 a federal judge struck down a zoning law, writing that its result was to "classify the population and segregate them according to their income." The Supreme Court reversed him in 1926. The cost in driving came later, when cities spread out.

slides.label: The long cleanup
slides.title: Undoing it takes new law
slides.text: In 2019 Oregon required its cities of more than 10,000 people to allow duplexes on land zoned for single-family homes, with deadlines in 2021 and 2022. It took a state law to change what local codes had fixed in place.

slides.label: The ledger
slides.title: Worth it?
gains: Light and air for streets under towers like the Equitable, whose shadow covered seven acres
A tool so useful that 218 municipalities with over 22 million people had zoning by the end of 1923
costs: A shortfall of more than 1.5 million homes, by one 2022 estimate
Homes, jobs and shops set far apart, so people rely on cars (EPA, 2001)
Districts closed to apartments in later codes; Oregon needed a 2019 state law to allow duplexes in them
slides.text: Zoning fixed real dangers in a crowded city. The rules it spread outlived the conditions they were written for.

slides.label: Credit for trying
slides.title: We owe him one
slides.text: Bassett took on real harms: dark streets, crowded tenements and factories next to homes. His code worked well enough that hundreds of cities copied it. Today's zoning reformers start by asking what those rules were for.

slides.label: How the pattern works
slides.title: The bill came with growth
slides.text: In 1916 the benefit was immediate: light, air and homes safe from factories. The cost arrived slowly, as cities grew outward under rules that kept homes, shops and jobs apart and made it hard to add homes where people wanted to live.

slides.label: How you do this
slides.title: Your rules send bills too
slides.text: After one bad release, your team rules that every change needs sign-off from three leads. Mistakes drop right away. Years later the team is five times bigger, and that rule is why nothing ships.
also: A cheap lease with a rent jump in year five
A pricing rule written for your first ten customers, applied to ten thousand

slides.label: Lessons
slides.title: What we take from it
items: A rule written for one city's problem becomes a template for places that never had it.
The costs of a rule can keep growing long after the people who wrote it are gone.
Courts and copycats can take a rule further than the person who wrote it.
